claims.text: A multiscale, defect-aware approach can predict bulk HfNbTaTiZr conductivity more accurately than conventional perfect-crystal analytical models.
The proposed accuracy advantage applies in both the near-0–200 K and 300–1200 K regimes.
The proposed approach applies to nominally pure bulk HfNbTaTiZr and material containing 1 wt.% oxygen.
Atomistic defect modeling can explicitly simulate scattering from intrinsic lattice defects and extrinsic oxygen sites.
Vacancies, dislocations, and oxygen impurity clusters are relevant structural imperfections in the modeled material.
Defects and oxygen impurity clusters modify the local electronic structure.
Defects and oxygen impurity clusters modify phonon scattering.
Explicit defect and impurity states account for additional electron-phonon and impurity-scattering processes.
These additional scattering processes are absent from ideal defect-free-crystal treatments.
Representing defect- and impurity-related scattering more realistically will improve agreement with measured conductivity across temperature.
The defect-aware model will predict conductivity to within approximately ±10% of experiment in both temperature regimes.
Perfect-crystal analytical approaches typically deviate from measurements by 20–30% when defects, including 1 wt.% oxygen, are present.
Conventional perfect-crystal predictions have shown significant deviations from measurements of real specimens.
The discrepancy of perfect-crystal predictions is especially important when oxygen impurities are present.
The proposed approach is applicable from near 0 K through 1200 K for HfNbTaTiZr containing approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
Predictions outside 0–1200 K or at impurity levels substantially different from 1 wt.% oxygen may not be accurate.
Prediction accuracy depends on the nature and spatial distribution of defects and oxygen.
Local microstructural variation could cause prediction errors larger than ±10%.

contradictions.description: The initial-state field claims applicability to both nominally pure and 1 wt.% oxygen material, whereas the boundary limits intended applicability to oxygen levels near 1 wt.% and warns that substantially different impurity levels may be inaccurate.
